assessment.name: AT2: Blues to Jazz
assessment.due: Part A Week 7, Part B Weeks 9 to 10

blueprint.title: 12-bar progression
blueprint.deck: The frame every blues in this unit is built on, in numbers rather than letters, so it moves to whatever key you compose in.
rules: Twelve bars, three systems of four: bar 1 is home (I), bar 5 moves away (IV), bar 9 pulls back (V).
The numbers do not change when the key does. Lesson 4 already asked you to prove that in three keys.
F is the class's shared key, written in small type under each numeral. Your own piece can sit in any key that suits the players in your band.

blueprint.title: Piano voicings
blueprint.deck: Four-note dominant 7th shapes for the chords the progression names: root, third, fifth and flattened seventh, stacked in that order.
rules: Play the shape as a block on beat 1 of the bar it belongs to, then leave space. Comping is not strumming through the whole bar.
The same four numbers build the chord in any key: 1, 3, 5, ♭7. F7, B♭7 and C7 are written out because they are this progression's three chords.
Guitar plays the same four notes on its own strings. Nobody in the rhythm section is exempt from knowing the shape.

blueprint.title: Drum pattern
blueprint.deck: One bar of swing feel: the ride pattern that carries the time, the hi-hat closing on beats 2 and 4, and the snare backbeat sitting with it.
rules: The ride is not four even quarter notes. It swings: long-short, long-short, twice a bar.
Hi-hat and snare land together, on beats 2 and 4. That is the backbeat, and it does not move.
Play the pattern from the notation once, then close the book and play it from memory. Lesson 15 is where that habit starts.

blueprint.title: Walking bass rules
blueprint.deck: Two rules, applied at every chord change: land on the root, and approach the next root by step or by semitone.
rules: Root on the change. The first note after a chord changes is always that chord's root, in reach of the hand that is about to play it.
Approach by step or by semitone. The note right before a change leads into the next root from a note or a semitone away, never a leap.
Everything between the root and the approach note is your choice: a scale step, a chord tone, a passing note. The two rules bound it; they do not fill it in for you.
Everybody in the band can play a walking line, at pitch or in octaves. Lesson 12 is not only for whoever plays bass.

lessons.title: The 12-bar blues, heard and counted
lessons.contentPoint: How genre and style are characterised
lessons.intention: We are learning to hear and count the 12-bar blues form.
criteria: I can count a 12-bar chorus and say where chords IV and V arrive.
steps: The 12-bar form heard in three recordings from the register, counted aloud, then diagrammed on the board.
How the genre is characterised: what makes a listener say this is a blues within two bars.
Students count a full chorus without the teacher and mark where the chord changes fall.
resources: Listening set from the repertoire register.
lessons.enduring: A genre is recognisable because of features that can be named.

body.lead: We are learning to hear and count the 12-bar blues form.

clauses.text: The 12-bar form heard in three recordings from the listening set, counted aloud together, then diagrammed on the board bar by bar.
How the genre is characterised: what makes a listener say “this is a blues” within two bars. Name the features rather than the feeling.
Count a full chorus without the teacher, and mark where the changes to chord IV and chord V fall.

criteria: I can count a 12-bar chorus without help.
I can say where chords IV and V arrive.

guide.brief: Two of the three songs, one measured chorus each. Press a name to play it from the top, or a time to drop into that moment.

cues.text: Bar one of a chorus. Chord **I** (F), and it holds for four bars before anything moves. Start counting here.
Bar five: the first move, up to chord **IV** (B♭), two bars before the form comes home again.
Bar nine: chord **V** (C) for a single bar, the sharpest pull in the whole form, then IV once more on the way back to I.
Bar one again, one full twelve-bar chorus later. Same three chords, same order, every time through.
Bar one, chord **I**, and this recording sits in E♭ rather than the E you might guess.
Bar nine, chord **V**, then back to IV before I lands again, same as the first song.
Bar one again. Faster than Sweet Home Chicago, so this chorus is over in under 23 seconds.

explain.title: Hearing a blues before you can see the chart

body.p: The twelve-bar blues is built from just three chords, I, IV and V, moved through in a fixed order every time. Once you know the order, counting a chorus stops being guesswork: it becomes counting to twelve, in fours, four times.

body.h: What tells you it's a blues in the first two bars

ul: **The chord itself, not just the note.** Chord I is usually a dominant seventh, not a plain major triad — there's a flattened seventh built into home itself, which is already a blues sound before anything else happens.
**Blue notes.** A flattened third or fifth leaning against the major chord underneath, played as an inflection rather than a clash.
**The shuffle.** Quavers played unevenly, long-short rather than even, so the groove has the same lean as the blue notes.
**The turnaround.** The last two bars almost always do something recognisable to point back to bar one, even before you've heard where bar one was.

body.p: None of this needs the chord chart in front of you. They are things a listener can hear inside two bars without it, which is exactly the skill this lesson asks for: recognise the genre by its features, then count the form underneath it.

lessons.title: Roman numerals I, IV and V
lessons.contentPoint: How genre and style are characterised
lessons.intention: We are learning to name chords by their function in the key.
criteria: I can label a progression with Roman numerals and transpose it.
steps: Roman numerals attached to chords the class already plays, then to the blues form.
Why numerals rather than letters: the form transposed to two more keys in the same lesson.
Written work: label the chords in three supplied progressions.
lessons.enduring: Naming a chord by its function is what lets a form move between keys.

body.lead: We are learning to name chords by what they do in the key.

clauses.text: Roman numerals go onto chords you already play, then onto the blues form. I is home, IV is the move away, V is the one that pulls back.
Why numerals and not letters: the same form is transposed into two more keys inside one lesson, and the numbers do not change.
Label the chords in three supplied progressions, then play one of them in a key you choose yourself.

criteria: I can label a progression with Roman numerals.
I can play the same progression in a new key.

body.p: You already know that a roman numeral names what a chord is doing rather than what it's called — chord I is home, wherever home happens to be. The blues uses three of those numbers: I, IV and V.

ul: **I is home.** Chord one, built on the key note. Where the form starts and where it always lands.
**IV moves away**, but gently — built a fourth above home, close enough that it never feels like it has left for good.
**V pulls.** Built a fifth above home, it is the chord with the strongest urge to resolve back to I, which is exactly why the form uses it right before the turnaround.

body.p: Change key and every letter name changes — I in C is C, I in G is G — but the numbers do not, because they describe a relationship, not a pitch. That is the whole reason a band can call “blues in Bb” and every player instantly knows the form without it being written out again: the numbers, not the letters, are what everyone already has memorised.

Labelling a progression is just naming each chord's number instead of its letter, and playing the same progression in a new key is the proof you actually understand the relationship, rather than just the shape under your fingers in one key alone.

lessons.title: The blues scale in the hands
lessons.contentPoint: Conventions of a period, genre or style
lessons.intention: We are learning to play the blues scale and hear its blue notes.
criteria: I can play the blues scale in one key and find the blue notes in it.
steps: The blues scale learned by playing it in one key across the room's instruments, then heard in the repertoire.
Blue notes located and bent or leaned on, so the sound is experienced before it is defined.
Call and response using only the scale, teacher to class.
lessons.enduring: The scale is a sound before it is a set of notes.

body.lead: We are learning to play the blues scale and hear the notes that make it sound like the blues.

clauses.text: The scale is learned by playing it, in one key, on whatever instrument you are on today.
The blue notes are found and then leaned on or bent, so you hear the sound before anybody defines it.
Call and response using the scale and nothing else. The teacher plays, you answer, and the backing does not stop.

criteria: I can play the blues scale in one key.
I can find the blue notes in it and make them sound blue.

body.p: The blues scale is the minor pentatonic with one extra note added: **1, b3, 4, #4, 5, b7**. Six notes, and every one of them is available over all three chords of the form without needing to change scale when the harmony moves to IV or V — which is part of why the blues works the way it does.

ul: **b3 and b7** clash gently against the major chord underneath, which is a dominant seventh chord built on a major third. That friction, not a mistake, is the blues sound.

**#4, the blue note proper,** sits right between IV and V. It is almost never held still — it is bent into or slid through on the way to a neighbouring note, which is why it barely counts as a fixed pitch at all.
**Leaning, not landing.** A blue note played dead in tune and held still stops sounding blue. The pitch is meant to move.

body.p: Write the six degrees onto whatever key you're playing in today, and the shape under your fingers stays the same the next time the class changes key — because you learned the relationships, not one fixed set of notes.

lessons.title: Aural routine: swing, syncopation and backbeat
lessons.contentPoint: How genre and style are characterised

body.lead: We are learning to hear and name the rhythmic features of this style.

clauses.text: The aural routine carries on from Term 1 with this term's content: straight quavers against swung ones, told apart by ear.

criteria: I can tell a swung excerpt from a straight one.
I can say what makes it swing.

explain.title: Swing, syncopation, backbeat: three separate things

body.p: These three get lumped together because they usually turn up in the same music, but they are three separate features, and a paper can ask about any one of them alone.

ul: **Swing** is a rhythmic feel: quavers played unevenly, the first of each pair held slightly longer than the second, instead of split evenly. It changes how the beat feels without changing which notes are played.
**Syncopation** is an accent landing where you don't expect it — off the beat, or on a normally weak part of the bar — so the rhythm pulls against the pulse rather than sitting on it.
**The backbeat** is a specific accent on beats 2 and 4 of a 4/4 bar, almost always carried by the snare drum. It is what makes you nod on the “off” beats rather than the strong ones.

body.p: A piece can swing without being syncopated, and can be heavily syncopated while played perfectly straight. Telling them apart by ear means asking three separate questions of what you're hearing — is the quaver pair even, is an accent in an unexpected place, is beat 2 and 4 marked — rather than one general impression of “groovy”.

patched.text: Listening set, work song and spiritual

explain.title: Call and response, before it had a name

body.p: The blues did not begin from nothing in the early twentieth century. It carries specific practices forward from West African musical traditions, transmitted through work songs and spirituals sung by enslaved and later free Black communities in the American South.

ul: **Call and response.** A leader sings or plays a phrase, a group answers it. It is a structural principle in many West African musical traditions, and it survives directly into the blues' leader-and-band phrasing, and into the way a blues vocal line is often answered by an instrumental fill.

**Blue notes.** The bent, leaned-on pitches that don't sit on a piano's fixed notes reflect vocal and instrumental inflections common in West African singing and playing, carried into instruments that were never built to make them.

**Work songs and spirituals.** Songs sung to coordinate labour, and songs of worship and endurance, carried rhythm, call and response and these vocal inflections together, and both are direct ancestors of the blues' own form and feel.

body.p: None of this is a footnote to the blues — it is the blues' actual history, carried forward by people who kept the practice alive under conditions designed to erase it. Naming where a feature came from is not optional colour on an analysis; for this style, it is part of getting the analysis right.

lessons.title: Composing the 16-bar blues: melody first
lessons.contentPoint: Sound sources and digital technologies
lessons.intention: We are learning to compose a melody over a given harmonic frame.
criteria: I can write a 16-bar melody that fits the progression and has a shape.
steps: Part A composition begins. Melody written first over the supplied progression, in flat.io.
Elements manipulated deliberately: register, rhythm, repetition and where the phrase ends.
Sound sources and playback used to test rather than to decorate.
resources: flat.io template with the progression already entered.
lessons.enduring: Composing inside a frame that already works is where the musical decisions become visible.

body.lead: We are learning to compose a melody over a frame that already works.

clauses.text: Part A starts today. The progression is already in your template, so the melody is what you write, and it goes on first.
Four decisions to make on purpose: register, rhythm, what repeats, and where the phrase stops.
Use playback to test what you wrote, not to decorate it. If it only works with the sound library, it is not written yet.

criteria: I can write a 16-bar melody that fits the progression.
I can give it a shape rather than a line of notes.

body.p: A melody is not just notes chosen one after another. It is answers to four decisions, made deliberately rather than landed on by accident.

ul: **Register.** Where the melody sits in pitch. Too high for all 16 bars and it's exhausting to sing or hard to hit cleanly; too low and it disappears under the band. Most melodies live within a register and only push to its edges for effect.

**Rhythm.** Whether the melody moves in long notes, short notes, or a mix, and whether it sits on the beat or pushes against it. This is often the first thing a listener notices, before the actual pitches.

**What repeats.** A melody with nothing repeated is hard to remember, and a melody that only repeats never goes anywhere. A phrase, or the shape of one, usually returns at least once, often changed slightly the second time.
**Where the phrase stops.** Phrases need somewhere to land — a long note, a rest, a return to a home pitch — so the listener can hear where one idea ends and the next begins.

body.p: Write with these four in mind and you can explain every choice in your own melody. Write without them and you can still end up with something that sounds fine, but you won't be able to say why it works, which is exactly what the rationale later in the term is going to ask you to do.

lessons.title: Writing the bass and the drum part
lessons.contentPoint: Writing for the performers' capabilities
lessons.intention: We are learning to write parts that the people in this room can play.

Writing for the capability of the actual player: range, hand position, and what is possible at tempo.

lessons.enduring: A composer writes for the performer, not for the page.

body.lead: We are learning to write parts that the people in this room can actually play.

clauses.text: Walking bass written with the supplied rules. The drum part entered from the supplied pattern, then varied.
Write for the player in front of you: their range, their hand position, and what is possible at your tempo.
Ask the classmate who will play each part. They are the reference, not the range chart.

criteria: I can write a bass part and a drum part for my piece.

explain.title: Writing for the hands that will actually play it

body.p: A walking bass line or a drum part is not finished when it looks right on the page. It's finished when the specific person playing it, on the instrument they actually have, can play it at tempo without needing three days to learn one bar.

ul: **Range.** A bass guitar's lowest open string is E, and a line that keeps dropping below it, or climbs so high it runs out of usable string, is not written for the instrument in the room. Check the bottom and the top against what the player can actually reach.

**Hand position.** A line that jumps around the neck constantly is harder to play in tempo than one that mostly stays in one position and moves out of it on purpose. Walking bass, especially, wants mostly stepwise or small-interval movement for exactly this reason.
**Tempo.** A pattern that is playable slowly can become impossible at the tempo the piece is actually meant to go. Test every part at full tempo, not just at the speed you wrote it in.

body.p: The check that actually matters is not whether the pattern looks correct against the rules you were given — it's whether the classmate who has to play it can. They are the reference, not the range chart, because a chart cannot tell you whether a particular stretch is comfortable in their hands.

steps: Revision workshop. Players and composers work in pairs, and the player reads the part aloud on their instrument.

body.lead: We are learning to work on each other's music respectfully and usefully.

clauses.text: Revision workshop. The player reads your part aloud on their instrument while you sit and listen to it.
